viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
Remarks from Anthropic CEO @DarioAmodei on our initial public offering:

My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind.

Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that, just a few years later, became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments.

So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket—tools for gene editing, gene synthesis, controlling brain cells with light—started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking. From intelligence.

Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress on other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades: it took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR.

Nature is full of these patterns. But we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them; too few scientists, with too little time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would’ve taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.

I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time. And although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe those processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by just a few years.

Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many others. Our customers—the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people—are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth; lift people out of poverty; protect democracy and free societies; even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them. And I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

At the same time, we have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation-states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable, but because we think they are avoidable.

Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and with public benefit has been woven into Anthropic’s DNA from the start. From safeguards against biological and cyber risks, to alignment training and testing, to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI systems.

There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us. The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed, even more so than it has already, towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and secure.

And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.

If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top. When the race to the top is working properly, it doesn’t matter which company has the best models—everyone wins because everyone is building safely. The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so, but the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.

The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better.

This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come. Starting today, we hope that you’ll join us on this mission.
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
Anthropic 首席执行官 @DarioAmodei 关于我们首次公开募股的评论：

我和我的联合创始人创立了 Anthropic，因为我们相信我们这个时代最强大的技术应该是为了造福人类而构建的。

丹妮拉和我的父亲因一种疾病去世，仅仅几年后，这种疾病就可以治愈。我的职业生涯始于生物学，希望能帮助未来的治愈方法早日到来。在实验室里，我看到了科学家在试图了解疾病和开发新疗法时所面临的巨大复杂性。

许多能够突破这一困境的科学工具——基因编辑、基因合成、用光控制脑细胞的工具——都是从纯粹的想法开始的。换句话说，它们来自于思考。来自智力。

人类智慧已经让世界上大部分地区的鼠疫、天花和脊髓灰质炎等疾病成为历史。但对于如此多的患者及其家人来说，其他疾病的进展太慢了。从一个伟大的想法到一种治疗方法可能需要数十年的时间：从首次发现 DNA 中奇怪的重复模式到第一个使用 CRISPR 治疗疾病的方法获得批准，花了很多年的时间。

大自然充满了这些模式。但我们的智慧太少，无法破译其中的大部分。科学家太少，时间太少。现在我们可以构建这种智能。无论是蛋白质折叠、药物设计、癌症遗传学还是临床试验管理，生物学和医学许多领域的科学家都发现克劳德可以帮助他们完成研究，所需时间只是几年前的一小部分。我相信足够强大的人工智能，与人类协同工作，可以将一个世纪的科学和医学进步压缩为十年。

我不想超越自己。目前我们所拥有的只是早期结果。实验和临床试验仍需要时间。尽管它们涉及缓慢而繁重的过程，但我相信人工智能可以大大加速这些过程。我们希望未来能有更少的家庭因仅仅几年的时间而错过治疗。

医学只是一个特别生动的例子，但还有很多其他例子。我们的客户——世界上最雄心勃勃的公司、非营利组织和个人——已经在应用我们构建的智能来刺激经济增长；让人们摆脱贫困；保护民主和自由社会；甚至让 DMV 等日常服务更好地运作。我们很自豪能与他们一起工作。我对我们未来可以一起做的事情非常乐观。

与此同时，我们一直诚实地认为这项技术存在非常现实的风险。这些问题包括个人或民族国家滥用技术、经济混乱、失去对人工智能系统的控制等。我们讨论这些风险不是因为我们认为它们是不可避免的，而是因为我们认为它们是可以避免的。

避免它们取决于构建人工智能的人们做出的选择。如果我们不关心安全，人工智能将会如何发展，而如果我们痴迷于安全，人工智能将会如何发展，两者之间存在着巨大的差异。对安全和公共利益的痴迷从一开始就融入了 Anthropic 的基因中。从防范生物和网络风险，到校准训练和测试，再到像 X 射线一样观察我们的模型，Anthropic 开创了理解和引导人工智能系统行为的方法。

任重而道远，最艰巨的安全工作还在后面。该公司拥有令人难以置信的人才，使我们能够构建最强大的人工智能系统，我们需要对其进行双重和三重检查，以确保这些人工智能系统的安全性，甚至比现在更加努力。

明确地说，我们将加快人工智能系统的训练和部署步伐，只要有必要，我们就确信它们是安全的，并将继续处于人类控制之下。我们不会屈服于商业或政治压力。今天，公司的财务状况变得更加强大，这样做只会增强我们做正确事情的决心。

如果我们能够证明我们可以在安全方面做出正确的选择，同时仍能打造一家极其成功的公司，那么我们行业的其他人也会受到启发，采取同样的做法。我们称之为登顶竞赛。当竞争顺利进行时，哪家公司拥有最好的模型并不重要——每个人都会赢，因为每个人都在安全地建造。当处于领先地位时，通往顶峰的竞争效果最好，我们完全希望并期望这样做，但目标是让整个行业变得更好，无论 Anthropic 在任何特定时间是赢还是输。

机器智能的出现是人类历史上的开创性时刻之一，我们有一个难得的机会来让它变得更好。

这一刻比任何一家公司或任何一个国家都重要。我们所有人都需要共同努力，才能确保这项技术为我们和子孙后代带来良好的发展。从今天开始，我们希望您能加入我们的行列。

viral_ticker_tweets.title: Our SVP @koraykv believes there won't be a single test or benchmark that tells us we've reached AGI. Instead, progress l

What if your profile picture was not just an NFT to display, but the identity of an AI agent you could actually control That is the concept behind

@meetmotes starts with its Genesis NFT collection, marked as coming soon, but the bigger idea 

goes beyond digital artwork. Each of the 20,000 Motes is designed to represent one agent identity, with the NFT acting as its public face and ownership reference

Here is how the structure connects:
One NFT represents one agent identity.

That identity is linked to its own smart account.

The owner funds the account with USDC and signs the permissions that govern the agent.

Those permissions define what the agent can trade, how much capital it can use, and when it must stop

The agent can only propose actions within the owner’s approved policy. Motes describes the policy as including valid targets, assets, 

limits, and an expiry window, while the account validates the signer and owner policy before execution.

paragraphs: An analysis of 10 million job postings by Bloomberg suggests that AI is putting additional pressure on China's already weak labor market. Entry-level workers and the creative industry in particular are reportedly already feeling the shift.

China's labor market has struggled for years with a sluggish economy, and AI now appears to be making things worse. According to a Bloomberg News analysis of nearly 10 million online job postings between July 2021 and June 2025, listings for jobs highly exposed to AI fell about 10 percentage points more than listings for less affected roles.

Bloomberg found that the total number of online job postings halved in the three years after June 2022, a starting point shortly before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and Chinese models like DeepSeek and ByteDance's Doubao rose to prominence. In nearly every industry, the decline hit jobs harder when their tasks overlapped heavily with AI capabilities, as measured by an index from Peking University. Bloomberg acknowledges, however, that the pure AI effect cannot be isolated with certainty because the broader economic slowdown may have hit office jobs disproportionately on its own.
### Chinese studies back up the findings

Two independent Chinese studies reached similar conclusions, according to Bloomberg. Data scientist Chen Qin of ShanghaiTech University analyzed 116 million online job postings and estimates that AI caused a net loss of 5.2% in new hires between 2023 and early 2026.

A study involving the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences goes even further, finding 21% fewer online job postings and 4% lower average wages. Bloomberg Economics estimates that roughly 70 million workers in China are at risk from AI disruption, compared with about 45 million in the US.

Chinese tech companies avoid citing AI openly as a reason for layoffs because they fear backlash from the government and the public, Bloomberg reports. Companies including Xiaomi, Meituan, and Alibaba's travel unit Fliggy have denied mass layoffs. Employees at large firms, however, have reported waves of cuts since spring that affected up to 30% of some departments.

Previously separate roles are also merging, according to Bloomberg. One Beijing-based internet company reportedly combined programming, design, and testing so that a single person using AI would take on the work of up to six people. Job postings from Tencent for an "AI Design Engineer"and from BlueFocus for an "AI Director"point in the same direction.
### AI micro-dramas are replacing film crews

According to Bloomberg, the shift is even more dramatic in Chinese micro-dramas, 90-second soap operas made for smartphones. Since the launch of new AI video generators like ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 in February, production time and costs have plummeted. Official data show that more than 90% of the 430,000 micro-dramas produced in the first eight months of 2026 were AI-generated. Linying Studio near Hangzhou, which opened only in late 2023, now sits mostly empty, and actresses like 26-year-old Zhang Ziqi report losing more than a third of their income.

According to the World Bank, China created only 21 million net new jobs in the five years through 2024, while youth unemployment reached nearly 19% over the summer. At the same time, more than 70 million college graduates are crowding into the job market, leading many to turn to retraining programs. China's leadership announced a nationwide survey on AI's labor-market effects in June, called for a "prudent pace,"and overhauled about a third of degree programs. Former central bank adviser Cai Fang nonetheless warns that the current situation is only a "temporary lull"before a bigger AI shock.

Similar patterns among entry-level workers are emerging outside China, though under different economic conditions. Stanford University researchers analyzed millions of US payroll records and found that employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed occupations has declined 13% in relative terms since late 2022, while experienced workers held steady. The decline was limited to occupations where AI directly automates tasks, which the researchers attribute to models mainly replacing formal textbook knowledge rather than hands-on experience.

In Australia, too, an analysis by the central bank found weaker employment figures and higher joblessness among 15- to 24-year-olds in highly exposed fields compared with older workers. Like Bloomberg, however, the bank cautioned against drawing causal conclusions too quickly, citing possible business-cycle and remote-work effects.

paragraphs: There was a dayslong Outlook outage. A nationwide ground stop for only the second time in 25 years. Banks seemed to suddenly stop working. Even iCloud couldn’t stay up and running. This week, it felt like the technological world simply collapsed. And it felt like this might be the beginning of something even bigger.

On this episode of The Vergecast, Nilay and David go through the week’s many calamities, and try to explain both what happened in each case — which was generally much milder than the conspiracy theories would have you believe — and why all these small issues might still add up to something worth worrying about. In a world filled with more AI and fewer humans, we’re going to see new kinds of problems and often struggle to find the fixes.

After that, the hosts discuss the latest in the Jensen Huang / Nvidia scandal, which is increasingly less about affairs and more about the allegedly very big business of illegally smuggling chips to China. Huang will not be back as Nvidia CEO anytime soon, no matter what a bunch of X users want, and the fallout of his exit seems likely to only increase.
Finally, in the lightning round, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, Nilay’s experience with his always-listening Apple Watch, Google’s inability to name products, and much more.

linked_tweets.content_zh:
开仓很容易，管理仓位却变得复杂。

任何使用过借贷协议的人都知道，这个头寸无法自行管理。

您必须跟踪抵押品，监控您的健康因素，了解剩余的借贷空间，并在市场状况变化时做出反应。

这种持续的责任是人工智能代理可以帮助解决的更有趣的问题之一。

@meetmotes 现已与 @aave 整合，将其代理扩展到去中心化借贷领域。

该集成引入了以下功能：

➠ 抵押品管理：随着贷款头寸的变化帮助管理抵押品。

➠ 借款和还款：自动化部分借款流程和还款。

➠ 健康因素监控：跟踪职位健康状况并应用自动化风险控制。

这与 Motes 特别相关的是与 Genesis NFT 的联系。

每个 Genesis NFT 都旨在将其所有者与专用 AI 代理联系起来，并在所有者定义的权限内运行个性化的 DeFi 策略。

我认为在评估自主财务时，风险管理与执行同样值得关注。

可以开仓的代理很有用。旨在监控抵押品、跟踪清算风险并在明确限制内运作的方案可以解决更大的问题。

随着 Aave 加入其整合，Motes 正在扩大其代理旨在处理的金融活动。

目标变得越来越清晰：通过所有者定义的控制进行自主执行。
linked_tweets.content_en:
Opening A Position Is Easy, Managing It Is Where Things Get Complicated.

Anyone who has used lending protocols knows the position doesn't manage itself.

You have to keep track of collateral, monitor your Health Factor, understand how much borrowing room remains and react when market conditions change.

That ongoing responsibility is one of the more interesting problems AI agents could help address.

@meetmotes has now integrated with @aave, extending its agents into decentralised lending and borrowing.

The integration introduces capabilities around:

➠ Collateral management: Helping manage collateral as lending positions evolve.

➠ Borrowing and repayment: Automating parts of the borrowing process and repayment.

➠ Health Factor monitoring: Tracking position health and applying automated risk controls.

What makes this particularly relevant to Motes is the connection to Genesis NFTs. 

Each Genesis NFT is designed to link its owner to a dedicated AI Agent, with personalised DeFi strategies operating within permissions defined by the owner.

I think risk management deserves just as much attention as execution when evaluating autonomous finance.

An agent that can open positions is useful. One designed to monitor collateral, track liquidation risk and operate within clear limits addresses a much bigger part of the problem.

With Aave joining its integrations, Motes is expanding the financial activities its agents are designed to handle.

The goal is becoming clearer: autonomous execution with owner-defined control.

linked_tweets.author: Florian Roth ⚡️
linked_tweets.content_zh:
我认为这次讨论存在重大误解。

开源软件中发现的漏洞数量不断增加并不一定意味着开源代码比专有软件更糟糕。

我们看到的是审查的大幅增加。

多年来，许多开源项目根本没有接受彻底的安全审查。没有人有时间、资源或经济动力来仔细观察。

现在，任何有权访问有能力的法学硕士的人都可以将其指向公共存储库并开始寻找漏洞。较新的模型非常擅长发现以前的工具和人工审核人员遗漏的问题。

但非常相似的事情正在幕后发生。

我可以根据我们自己的经验以及与其他软件公司人员的讨论告诉您，内部开发团队也在努力应对人工智能辅助代码审查的大量发现。

其中许多发现涉及已在生产环境中运行多年的代码。在专有软件开发中，它们很少成为公共 CVE 或安全公告。它们最终会成为 Jira 票证，造成积压，需要数周或数月的时间才能处理。

具有讽刺意味的是，虽然人工智能加速了软件开发，但它也暴露了多年来积累的技术债务和以前没有人发现的安全问题，从而减慢了团队的速度。

因此，我会谨慎地将当前的开源漏洞浪潮解释为代码质量较低的证据。
linked_tweets.content_en:
I think there’s a major misunderstanding in this discussion.

The growing number of vulnerabilities discovered in open source software doesn’t necessarily mean that open source code is worse than proprietary software.

What we’re seeing is a massive increase in scrutiny.

For years, many open source projects simply didn’t receive thorough security reviews. Nobody had the time, resources or financial incentive to look that closely.

Now anyone with access to a capable LLM can point it at a public repository and start looking for vulnerabilities. And newer models are getting remarkably good at finding issues that previous tools and human reviewers missed.

But something very similar is happening behind closed doors.

I can tell you from our own experience, and from discussions with people at other software companies, that internal development teams are also struggling with a flood of findings from AI-assisted code reviews.

Many of these findings concern code that has been running in production for years. In proprietary software development, they rarely become public CVEs or security advisories. They end up as Jira tickets, creating backlogs that take weeks or months to process.

Ironically, while AI accelerates software development, it’s also slowing teams down by exposing years of accumulated technical debt and security issues that nobody had identified before.

So I’d be careful about interpreting the current wave of open source vulnerabilities as evidence of lower code quality.

news.title_en: Bloomberg analysis of 10 million job postings shows AI-exposed roles in China fell 10 percentage points faster than others
news.author: Maximilian Schreiner
news.content_snippet:
An analysis of 10 million job postings by Bloomberg suggests that AI is putting additional pressure on China's already weak labor market. Entry-level workers and the creative industry in particular are reportedly already feeling the shift.

China's labor market has struggled for years with a sluggish economy, and AI now appears to be making things worse. According to a Bloomberg News analysis of nearly 10 million online job postings between July 2021 and June 2025, listings for jobs highly expos
news.summary_en: of nearly 10 million job postings reveals that AI is significantly disrupting China's labor market, disproportionately affecting entry-level and creative roles. Vulnerable positions have seen a demand decline 10 percentage points sharper than non-impacted roles, with research from ShanghaiTech University and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences confirming structural shifts including role consolidation and quiet staff reductions at major internet firms.
paragraphs: An analysis of 10 million job postings by Bloomberg suggests that AI is putting additional pressure on China's already weak labor market. Entry-level workers and the creative industry in particular are reportedly already feeling the shift.

China's labor market has struggled for years with a sluggish economy, and AI now appears to be making things worse. According to a Bloomberg News analysis of nearly 10 million online job postings between July 2021 and June 2025, listings for jobs highly exposed to AI fell about 10 percentage points more than listings for less affected roles.

Bloomberg found that the total number of online job postings halved in the three years after June 2022, a starting point shortly before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and Chinese models like DeepSeek and ByteDance's Doubao rose to prominence. In nearly every industry, the decline hit jobs harder when their tasks overlapped heavily with AI capabilities, as measured by an index from Peking University. Bloomberg acknowledges, however, that the pure AI effect cannot be isolated with certainty because the broader economic slowdown may have hit office jobs disproportionately on its own.
### Chinese studies back up the findings

Two independent Chinese studies reached similar conclusions, according to Bloomberg. Data scientist Chen Qin of ShanghaiTech University analyzed 116 million online job postings and estimates that AI caused a net loss of 5.2% in new hires between 2023 and early 2026.

A study involving the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences goes even further, finding 21% fewer online job postings and 4% lower average wages. Bloomberg Economics estimates that roughly 70 million workers in China are at risk from AI disruption, compared with about 45 million in the US.

Chinese tech companies avoid citing AI openly as a reason for layoffs because they fear backlash from the government and the public, Bloomberg reports. Companies including Xiaomi, Meituan, and Alibaba's travel unit Fliggy have denied mass layoffs. Employees at large firms, however, have reported waves of cuts since spring that affected up to 30% of some departments.

Previously separate roles are also merging, according to Bloomberg. One Beijing-based internet company reportedly combined programming, design, and testing so that a single person using AI would take on the work of up to six people. Job postings from Tencent for an "AI Design Engineer"and from BlueFocus for an "AI Director"point in the same direction.
### AI micro-dramas are replacing film crews

According to Bloomberg, the shift is even more dramatic in Chinese micro-dramas, 90-second soap operas made for smartphones. Since the launch of new AI video generators like ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 in February, production time and costs have plummeted. Official data show that more than 90% of the 430,000 micro-dramas produced in the first eight months of 2026 were AI-generated. Linying Studio near Hangzhou, which opened only in late 2023, now sits mostly empty, and actresses like 26-year-old Zhang Ziqi report losing more than a third of their income.

According to the World Bank, China created only 21 million net new jobs in the five years through 2024, while youth unemployment reached nearly 19% over the summer. At the same time, more than 70 million college graduates are crowding into the job market, leading many to turn to retraining programs. China's leadership announced a nationwide survey on AI's labor-market effects in June, called for a "prudent pace,"and overhauled about a third of degree programs. Former central bank adviser Cai Fang nonetheless warns that the current situation is only a "temporary lull"before a bigger AI shock.

Similar patterns among entry-level workers are emerging outside China, though under different economic conditions. Stanford University researchers analyzed millions of US payroll records and found that employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed occupations has declined 13% in relative terms since late 2022, while experienced workers held steady. The decline was limited to occupations where AI directly automates tasks, which the researchers attribute to models mainly replacing formal textbook knowledge rather than hands-on experience.

In Australia, too, an analysis by the central bank found weaker employment figures and higher joblessness among 15- to 24-year-olds in highly exposed fields compared with older workers. Like Bloomberg, however, the bank cautioned against drawing causal conclusions too quickly, citing possible business-cycle and remote-work effects.

The Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, established by Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) co-founder Jensen Huang and his wife, plans to spend $350 million on computing time from CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV).

The commitment is by far the foundation's largest gift last year, and an earlier Nvidia filing showed $108.3 million had already been spent. It donated about $373 million in total, roughly three times its 2024 giving.

The money supports the Computing Initiative for Open Science, which gives research grant recipients access to large-scale graphics processing unit, or GPU, computing power, the filing said. A CoreWeave spokesperson said the foundation does not use the computing itself, and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.

The arrangement adds to concerns about circular financing, in which chip suppliers such as Nvidia invest in customers, which may create artificial demand. Nvidia is a major CoreWeave shareholder, and Huang defended the company after its shares slumped on concerns about debt-funded hardware spending.
Its assets reached $12.7 billion at the end of 2025, up from $9.2 billion a year earlier, with Nvidia shares making up nearly 90%.

Anthropic PBC shares erased much of their first-day jump on Friday, testing investors’ faith after the AI lab delivered the biggest initial public offering in history.

Shares in the company behind the Claude chatbot plunged as low as $87.26 each in early trading in its second day as a public company, trimming the gain from the IPO price of $83 to as little as 5.1%. The stock popped just after opening on Thursday, briefly lifting Anthropic’s market value above Amazon.com Inc.’s, before beginning its slide.

The drop came at the same time as the so-called over-allotment option, also known as a greenshoe, was exercised, allowing the underwriting banks to sell additional shares. The over-allotment lifted the total raised by Anthropic and the co-founders selling shares in the offering to $119.5 billion, with $93.5 billion in the IPO and $26 billion from the concurrent private placement.

The trading gives Anthropic a market value of about $1.5 trillion, ranking it among the 15 biggest publicly traded companies in the world. Stocks were roiled by a selloff that spread from Asia to the US, with the Nasdaq 100 Index falling 1.5% and the S&P 500 Index sinking 0.5%.
“There’s a buyers’ strike for Anthropic as well as the wider AI and tech trade,” according to Emmanuel Valavanis of Forte Securities.

“There are many clients who appear to have been left without allocations and, having been left out of the party, aren’t prepared to pick up the pieces from the hangover. With no skin in the game, and no index considerations for risk of relative performance, investors can sit on the sidelines and wait for longer term price discovery rather than risk getting caught out.”

Anthropic’s IPO made history not only because of its size, but also because the company is the first frontier AI model maker to go public. The trading represents a test of whether investors have appetite for companies pioneering the technology itself, rather than the tools to develop it such as chips and data centers. It also sets up a debut for rival OpenAI, which isn’t planning to go public before 2027.

The IPO delivered outsize returns to its backers and pushing up the combined wealth of its seven founders to $166 billion. The fundraise eclipsed the record set in June by SpaceX’s IPO, which ultimately totaled $86.2 billion. Goldman Sachs Group Inc., Morgan Stanley and 20 other banks earned a record $550 million in fees for their work on Anthropic’s IPO.

“We are impressed by the wealth creation this company is generating, in a matter of a few years and with reasonable free cash flow burn,” said Raphael Thuin, head of capital markets strategies at Tikehau Capital.
“To get exposed to AI though, we tend to favor more diversified businesses, and in any case we would like to see the post IPO volatility fade before engaging further.”

Anthropic won over investors with a focus on enterprise customers, propelling its run-rate revenue — a measure annualized from a shorter period — to $81 billion as of Oct. 31, up $10 billion from the end of September, its regulatory filings show.

Claude Code, the company’s coding agent for software developers, is widely adopted in the industry and has even been used by NASA engineers, the filing shows. Anthropic has more than 11,900 customers delivering $100,000 of revenue each on a trailing 12-month basis as of the end of September, up from about 1,500 in 2025.

Investors considering taking stakes may decide to wait out the market turmoil first. The Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, spiked to more than 29 on Friday morning, well above the level where companies typically consider the market welcoming to IPOs.
“We would look at buying in the open market if the stock get close or even below the IPO price,” said Olivier David, a fund manager at Vega IS.

Anthropic’s listing joins companies linked to AI that have pushed US IPO volume to an all-time high. Including Anthropic, first time stock sales raised $258 billion this year, beating 2021’s $195 billion haul, excluding financial vehicles such as blank-check firms, data compiled by Bloomberg show. paragraphs: After Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google launched their own AI agents, Apple is now building one too - while making it harder for rivals to access its devices. According to a job listing, Apple is hiring a senior engineer to lead the project as a rival to Muse, Dots, Duet, and Grok Bots. Privacy is expected to be central to the new agent, with permission models and sandboxing (protected test environments).

According to Bloomberg, the agent could arrive as early as late next year, though it remains in an early stage. Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is pushing software chief Craig Federighi toward a bolder AI strategy, the report says. After many delays, the company recently rolled out generative AI features for Siri. The road to that release was marked by internal rifts and staff departures.

Meanwhile, macOS 27.3 now requires 14 steps instead of four for users to let third-party agents like ChatGPT control their Macs. Apple says the change protects users, though some AI companies and users see it as an effort to slow down competitors, Bloomberg reports.

news.author: Maximilian Schreiner
news.content_snippet:
Nvidia is nearing a deal to acquire AI startup Inception for at least $500 million. That's according to three people familiar with the talks told The Information. The deal also includes performance bonuses for the more than 30 employees at the two-year-old San Francisco Bay Area startup.

Inception builds language models using the diffusion process known from image generation. Rather than generating responses token by token like the conventional models behind ChatGPT and Claude, they refine a fu
news.summary_en: Nvidia is in advanced talks to acquire AI startup Inception for at least $500 million, including full-time integration of founders Stefano Ermon, Aditya Grover, and Volodymyr Kuleshov. Inception specializes in diffusion-based language models, such as Mercury 3, which refine responses globally rather than token-by-token. This acquisition is designed to enhance Nvidia's Nemotron open-source lineup and accelerate its physical simulation capabilities for robotics.
paragraphs: Nvidia is nearing a deal to acquire AI startup Inception for at least $500 million. That's according to three people familiar with the talks told The Information. The deal also includes performance bonuses for the more than 30 employees at the two-year-old San Francisco Bay Area startup.

Inception builds language models using the diffusion process known from image generation. Rather than generating responses token by token like the conventional models behind ChatGPT and Claude, they refine a full response step by step. The startup most recently released Mercury 3.

The acquisition aims to bolster Nvidia's open-source Nemotron models and physical models for robots, helping it compete with OpenAI and Anthropic as both build their own inference chips. Palantir and US government agencies already use Nemotron as an alternative to Chinese models. Talks began before Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and after Microsoft expressed interest. Inception co-founders and professors Stefano Ermon, Aditya Grover, and Volodymyr Kuleshov are expected to join Nvidia full time. Neither company initially commented.
We covered Inception's approach alongside 40 other neolabs in our latest AI Radar #5.

paragraphs: There was a dayslong Outlook outage. A nationwide ground stop for only the second time in 25 years. Banks seemed to suddenly stop working. Even iCloud couldn’t stay up and running. This week, it felt like the technological world simply collapsed. And it felt like this might be the beginning of something even bigger.

On this episode of The Vergecast, Nilay and David go through the week’s many calamities, and try to explain both what happened in each case — which was generally much milder than the conspiracy theories would have you believe — and why all these small issues might still add up to something worth worrying about. news.title_en: Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment
news.author: Ashley Capoot
news.content_snippet:
Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering, bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release on Friday.

The artificial intelligence company raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and net an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June.

Anthropic said it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at $83 per share in the off
news.summary_en: AI firm Anthropic completed its historic IPO on Nasdaq, raising a total of $93.5 billion after underwriters exercised the greenshoe option for an additional $12.2 billion. Simultaneously, the company closed a $26 billion private placement involving major tech entities like AMD, Google, Microsoft, and Nvidia, bringing total gross proceeds to $119.5 billion.
paragraphs: Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering, bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release on Friday.
The artificial intelligence company raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and net an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June.

Anthropic said it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at $83 per share in the offering. It sold 980 million shares on Wednesday and its underwriters had the option to purchase up to an additional 147 million shares by Friday as part of the overallotment, which is commonly referred to as the "greenshoe."

Shares of the Claude maker opened trading at $111.50 on the Nasdaq Thursday, but slid throughout the day and closed at $97.17. The stock sank 12% in pre-market trading on Friday during a broad tech sell-off.

In addition to the sale of its Class A common stock, Anthropic closed a concurrent sale of its Class N common stock after a group of tech companies, including Advanced Micro Devices, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and others, agreed to participate in a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price. Anthropic said Friday that aggregate gross proceeds from its IPO, including the private placement, totaled $119.5 billion, before deducting offering expenses.

Anthropic dodged an unforgiving series of obstacles on its road to the Nasdaq on Thursday, as investors brooded over Jensen Huang's shocking ouster at Nvidia, voters' stinging rebuke of the tech during the midterms and whether rising interest rates would stymie industry plans for a multi-trillion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout.

CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a handful of other researchers, including his sister Daniela, quit their jobs at OpenAI, now Anthropic's chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, which have captivated the corporate world and fueled the company's historic rise.
The siblings celebrated the IPO as a "milestone"in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, but said there's more work ahead for Anthropic.

"For us, it's like one stop on the journey,"Daniela Amodei said. "We think about this as, 'Wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company.'"

news.author: Matthias Bastian

paragraphs: Google is rolling out a collapsible sidebar globally on its Desktop Search homepage, making AI search even easier to access. Announced on X by Google Search VP Robby Stein, the feature lets users easily find and reopen recent AI searches. Sitting on the left side of the AI Mode interface, it lets users start new threads, search existing ones, create notebooks, and open recent queries and settings.

Stein said people are increasingly asking Google Search questions that a single query can't answer. In testing, the sidebar significantly helped users make progress and keep researching across the web by making it easier to pick up right where they left off. The update also pushes Google's shift toward an AI answer engine.

Google is also rolling out temporary threads in AI Mode worldwide. These searches don't use prior context, aren't saved to history, and don't affect future recommendations. Once closed, they're gone, Stein said.

paragraphs: Uber has opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities as the company tests whether there’s a market for shuttling tweens without an adult by their side. The program, called Uber Kids, launched quietly over the past few weeks in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee, and Madison, Wisconsin.

The program, which builds on Uber’s existing teen ride-hailing service for passengers ages 13 to 17, is the latest bid by Uber to expand its customer base. Uber is describing this as a limited pilot program, which means it may never expand beyond these cities or even exist by next year. But if successful, it could open up a potentially lucrative market for Uber: busy families with active kids.

The Uber Kids program is stacked with mandatory requirements for parents and drivers. Parents or guardians are the only ones who can order a ride for their child, which they can do by adding the child to their family profile and completing a mandatory onboarding that explains the built-in safety features. A parent or guardian must be present at the pickup locations for the trip to begin and also have to include a note to the driver that explains the drop off.

Meanwhile, only highly rated drivers who have been invited are allowed to participate. Those drivers are required to complete an education module that includes step-by-step instructions and must be opted into live video streaming so parents can watch the trip in real time, according to Uber.

Uber said it also requires PIN verification for every Uber Kids trip, and says all recordings will be encrypted and not available to the driver, and will use sensors and GPS data to detect if the ride goes off course, stops unexpectedly, or ends early.

Drivers who are willing to adhere to those rules to shuttle kids will get a pay bump for the effort, according to Uber. Eligible drivers will earn $7 more on every Uber Kids trip compared to a standard one, the company says on the dedicated Uber Kids web page. Drivers will receive an extra $20 for the first Uber Kids ride they complete.

The extra compensation underscores a key challenge Uber faces as it expands into this younger age group — how to convince drivers to take on that added responsibility. If the program does expand it could eventually compete with existing transportation services such as HopSkipDrive and Zum.

Uber opened its ride-hailing service to minors in 2023 when it launched Uber for Teens, although the company had conducted early pilots several years prior. As the program expanded nationwide, Uber introduced a live video streaming feature.

[Root Cause & Mechanism] Traditional performance-based incentives have lost efficacy due to the rapid wealth accumulation of employees
[Key Metrics] Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported.
[Industry Impact & Outlook] Such management styles risk talent attrition, potentially weakening the company's long-term R&D moat.
paragraphs: As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.

He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.

This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Mr. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”

The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Mr. Huang’s management style.
“I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said.

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously.

Mr. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Thousands have signed a letter asking for his return. Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Mr. Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. He cultivated loyalty through not just his technical mastery but also acts of personal compassion and praise. But he ruled through fear.

Mr. Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Mr. Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability.

Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Mr. Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career. Mr. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Mr. Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times.
Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Mr. Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported.

Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993.

Some managers followed Mr. Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.)

Mr. Huang denied Mr. Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Mr. Fisher said. Mr. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Mr. Huang’s behavior.

Nvidia declined to comment. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Mr. Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Mr. Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Mr. Huang once belittled Ms. Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Mr. Huang.

Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. He was also beloved. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone.

Mr. Huang had a similar effect on his staff. He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A.I. boom.

Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Mr. Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Mr. Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave.
But in the eyes of some, Mr. Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards.

In September 2004, Mr. Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources. A longtime human resources executive who previously worked at Merrill Lynch and Motorola, Mr. Winston was soon taken aback by the disarray of the H.R. department and the cultural norms of Nvidia. This account of his time at the company is based on interviews and Mr. Winston’s notes and emails, as well as drafts of a lawsuit and other legal documents reviewed by The Times.
In his first days at Nvidia, he learned that two key human resources leaders had just quit and others were on the verge of resigning.
That October, at a two-day off-site meeting attended by about 50 employees, Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang unleashed graphic violent threats.
“You have to do this, or I will rip your fucking heart out and stomp on it,” Mr. Huang said at one point.

“I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.”

Mr. Winston said other attendees were “terrorized” and pleaded with him to intervene. Days later, he voiced his concerns during a meeting with top executives. One told him that the conduct was typical but could be a liability for the company. Another advised him to “toughen up.”

Mr. Winston said he then confronted Mr. Huang, warning him that he had “crossed the line” and that mistreating employees could expose Nvidia to lawsuits. He said Mr. Huang dismissed the concerns and defended public humiliation as a “rite of passage.” Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang bragged to him that he subjected new employees to it during their first six months at the company to test whether they would stand for it.
Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Mr. Huang told him.

That November, Mr. Winston was called into a meeting with Mr. Huang and another executive, who then fired him. Mr. Huang told Mr. Winston that he was “not a good fit.” If Mr. Winston sued Nvidia, Mr. Huang said he would make sure Mr. Winston never worked in Silicon Valley again.
“To say Nvidia fired me because it just was not ‘a fit’ is nothing more than a smokescreen,” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “The real issue,” he wrote, was Mr. Huang’s “unconscionable behavior.”

In the months that followed, Mr. Winston filed a formal complaint against Nvidia with California’s Department of Fair Employment and Housing, making allegations that he was fired for opposing Mr. Huang’s treatment of employees, including what he said constituted sexual harassment. Mr. Winston then drafted a lawsuit against Nvidia and Mr. Huang.
But before the complaint was filed, both sides reached a settlement. Neither side admitted liability or wrongdoing.
Mr. Winston rejoined the banking industry, and later blew the whistle against Countrywide Financial Corporation for its conduct during the buildup to the financial crisis. He died earlier this year.

In 2007, Stephen Pettigrew, a former lawyer for the company, sued Nvidia over claims that included age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Mr. Winston’s allegations of sexual harassment. Mr. Pettigrew reported in a complaint filed with the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing that he sought “emergency medical attention for severe nervous tension and anxiety, as a direct result of the actions of Nvidia.”

Mr. Pettigrew discussed Mr. Winston’s complaint during depositions for his own lawsuit, citing Mr. Winston’s allegations as evidence of misconduct that exposed Nvidia to legal risk. Nvidia’s general counsel at the time, David Shannon, confirmed during another deposition in the case that Mr. Winston’s dispute was resolved in a pre-litigation financial settlement.

Nvidia denied all wrongdoing, and said that Mr. Pettigrew was fired for poor performance. The company countersued, saying that he breached his contract and misused company documents. The case ultimately settled out of court in 2009.

After Nvidia’s chips were used in 2012 to train an early artificial intelligence system, Mr. Huang concluded that the future of computing would be A.I. Employees recall receiving his email on a Friday saying the company was pivoting its business from graphics to deep learning, a precursor to A.I. He froze hiring for anybody but experts in that field, and Nvidia became an A.I. chipmaker overnight.

A decade later, Mr. Huang’s bet paid off when ChatGPT arrived, kick-starting frenzied interest and investment in A.I. Demand for Nvidia’s chips skyrocketed, and the company’s value soared. Many of the company’s 42,000 employees became fabulously wealthy and were exhilarated to be at the forefront of a technology Mr. Huang referred to as the next Industrial Revolution.

In the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation, some employees have shared stories of a boss who went out of his way to support them. Last week, Vartika Singh, who works on strategy at Nvidia, recalled Mr. Huang’s support when her sister had brain cancer.

“Thank you, Jensen,” Ms. Singh wrote in a social media post. “For your guidance, for believing in people and ideas long before the rest of us understood them, and above all, for your extraordinary humanity.”

Mr. Huang’s mix of disparagement and motivation created something akin to Stockholm syndrome, six current and former employees said. The phenomenon, in which somebody held captive develops an emotional bond with their abuser, mirrored their relationship with Mr. Huang, they said.

Rather than fire people, Mr. Huang sometimes preferred to further humiliate them. When Ned Finkle, his former vice president of strategic marketing, faltered in a meeting with a major customer, Mr. Huang chewed him out in front of executives from the other company, said two people who spoke anonymously about the private exchange.

Mr. Huang then named Mr. Finkle vice president of external affairs, or government relations. At the time, Mr. Huang considered it one of the least important jobs at Nvidia, the two people said. Mr. Finkle did not respond to requests for comment.
Mr. Huang’s tirades continued until the end.

He usually did not meet one-on-one with subordinates because, he has publicly said, such meetings reduced transparency within Nvidia. But top executives considered the move a power play that gave Mr. Huang more control. If anyone disagreed with Mr. Huang, they would have to do so in front of a group. Mr. Huang could then fire back, ridiculing that person in front of everyone else.
Mr. Huang also ripped into longtime leaders in front of their own teams, telling them their boss was incompetent and unqualified, two people said.

In one instance, Mr. Huang went around a room, telling managers he would kill them, according to one person with knowledge of the incident. When he reached a person in their 70s, Mr. Huang said that the person was really old and everyone hoped they would drop dead.

Mr. Huang also made personal attacks. He once made fun of an executive who had taken his children camping and said he needed to find a more committed employee for the job, according to one person. He often mocked another executive for enjoying aviation as a hobby, two people said.

In 2019, after Nvidia lost a bid to help build a U.S. government supercomputer, Mr. Huang castigated a sales executive in front of government officials for missing out on part of a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The executive then threw his employee badge at Mr. Huang, who said he accepted the executive’s resignation on the spot, according to two people with knowledge of the incident.

Mr. Huang’s behavior rubbed off on other senior leaders at the company, including his daughter, Madison. On one call last year with Nvidia’s marketing team, Ms. Huang repeatedly berated a vice president, who then left the call, according to a recording of the meeting reviewed by The Times.
“I’m having an anxiety attack,” the vice president said. “I’m going to drop off. I’m sorry.”
Ms. Huang did not respond to requests for comment.

As Nvidia became the linchpin of the A.I. boom, Mr. Huang’s conduct started to spill outside the company. At Nvidia’s developer conference earlier this year, Mr. Huang moderated a panel with business partners, including Arthur Mensch, the chief executive of the French A.I. start-up Mistral.
During the panel, Mr. Huang interrupted Mr. Mensch several times, apparently taking issue with the Mistral chief executive’s French accent, according to two people who watched the talk.
“You’re not even speaking human,” Mr. Huang said at one point, before another panelist intervened. A spokesman for Mistral declined to comment.
Daniel Gutierrez, an A.I. researcher and longtime “Jensen fan” who was watching the panel, said the interaction changed his perspective on Mr. Huang.

“I thought in the moment, what is happening right now that’s causing you to attack this poor guy?” Mr. Gutierrez said. “When all the new stuff happened in the last week, I go, wait a minute now. Maybe Jensen isn’t the guy I thought I revered.”

Employees recall receiving his email on a Friday saying the company was pivoting its business from graphics to deep learning, a precursor to A.I. He froze hiring for anybody but experts in that field, and Nvidia became an A.I. chipmaker overnight.

A decade later, Mr. Huang’s bet paid off when ChatGPT arrived, kick-starting frenzied interest and investment in A.I. Demand for Nvidia’s chips skyrocketed, and the company’s value soared. Many of the company’s 42,000 employees became fabulously wealthy and were exhilarated to be at the forefront of a technology Mr. Huang referred to as the next Industrial Revolution.

In the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation, some employees have shared stories of a boss who went out of his way to support them. Last week, Vartika Singh, who works on strategy at Nvidia, recalled Mr. Huang’s support when her sister had brain cancer.

“Thank you, Jensen,” Ms. Singh wrote in a social media post. “For your guidance, for believing in people and ideas long before the rest of us understood them, and above all, for your extraordinary humanity.”

Mr. Huang’s mix of disparagement and motivation created something akin to Stockholm syndrome, six current and former employees said. The phenomenon, in which somebody held captive develops an emotional bond with their abuser, mirrored their relationship with Mr. Huang, they said.

Rather than fire people, Mr. Huang sometimes preferred to further humiliate them. When Ned Finkle, his former vice president of strategic marketing, faltered in a meeting with a major customer, Mr. Huang chewed him out in front of executives from the other company, said two people who spoke anonymously about the private exchange.

Mr. Huang then named Mr. Finkle vice president of external affairs, or government relations. At the time, Mr. Huang considered it one of the least important jobs at Nvidia, the two people said. Mr. Finkle did not respond to requests for comment.
Mr. Huang’s tirades continued until the end.

He usually did not meet one-on-one with subordinates because, he has publicly said, such meetings reduced transparency within Nvidia. But top executives considered the move a power play that gave Mr. Huang more control. If anyone disagreed with Mr. Huang, they would have to do so in front of a group. Mr. Huang could then fire back, ridiculing that person in front of everyone else.
Mr. Huang also ripped into longtime leaders in front of their own teams, telling them their boss was incompetent and unqualified, two people said.

In one instance, Mr. Huang went around a room, telling managers he would kill them, according to one person with knowledge of the incident. When he reached a person in their 70s, Mr. Huang said that the person was really old and everyone hoped they would drop dead.

Mr. Huang also made personal attacks. He once made fun of an executive who had taken his children camping and said he needed to find a more committed employee for the job, according to one person. He often mocked another executive for enjoying aviation as a hobby, two people said.

In 2019, after Nvidia lost a bid to help build a U.S. government supercomputer, Mr. Huang castigated a sales executive in front of government officials for missing out on part of a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The executive then threw his employee badge at Mr. Huang, who said he accepted the executive’s resignation on the spot, according to two people with knowledge of the incident.

Mr. Huang’s behavior rubbed off on other senior leaders at the company, including his daughter, Madison. On one call last year with Nvidia’s marketing team, Ms. Huang repeatedly berated a vice president, who then left the call, according to a recording of the meeting reviewed by The Times.
“I’m having an anxiety attack,” the vice president said. “I’m going to drop off. I’m sorry.”
Ms. Huang did not respond to requests for comment.

As Nvidia became the linchpin of the A.I. boom, Mr. Huang’s conduct started to spill outside the company. At Nvidia’s developer conference earlier this year, Mr. Huang moderated a panel with business partners, including Arthur Mensch, the chief executive of the French A.I. start-up Mistral.
During the panel, Mr. Huang interrupted Mr. Mensch several times, apparently taking issue with the Mistral chief executive’s French accent, according to two people who watched the talk.
“You’re not even speaking human,” Mr. Huang said at one point, before another panelist intervened. A spokesman for Mistral declined to comment.
Daniel Gutierrez, an A.I. researcher and longtime “Jensen fan” who was watching the panel, said the interaction changed his perspective on Mr. Huang.

“I thought in the moment, what is happening right now that’s causing you to attack this poor guy?” Mr. Gutierrez said. “When all the new stuff happened in the last week, I go, wait a minute now. Maybe Jensen isn’t the guy I thought I revered.”

news.title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
news.title_en: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
news.author: Jess Weatherbed
news.content_snippet: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents
news.summary_en: Meredith Whittaker, President of Signal, announced that integrated OS-level AI agents undermine app-level privacy. To mitigate this, Signal has disabled screenshot functionality on iOS and Android to prevent AI assistants from harvesting encrypted message data, while demanding that OS providers implement transparent technical controls for developer-side AI access management.
paragraphs: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.

“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.”

Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device filesystem.

Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data.

“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

news.title: Muse Is Unleashing a World of Pettiness on Instagram
news.title_en: Muse Is Unleashing a World of Pettiness on Instagram
news.author: Jason Parham
news.content_snippet:

news.summary_en: Meta's AI assistant Muse is being widely utilized by users to execute automated, bulk unfollow operations. The tool accurately identifies non-reciprocal followers and generates detailed category lists, while mitigating the risk of account suspension typically associated with third-party automated scripts.
paragraphs: Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

“I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old New Yorker tells WIRED. But after realizing that by using Muse, his account wouldn’t get flagged as spam, his mind was made up. “I was like, I actually will be a little petty.”

After downloading Muse, Roberts, who had over 7,600 followers, entered the prompt: “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on instagram and can you unfollow them for me. ”

Within minutes, Muse identified 151 accounts. It attached an Excel sheet with a breakdown of everyone cataloged—separated by categories identifying their username, real name, classification, and profile link—and asked if Roberts wanted to proceed with his request. Shockingly, some of the names were people he thought of as friends. “It was a little surprising, but also a reminder that we don’t have a relationship anymore.”

Following the success of his November 7 cleanse, Roberts posted about it on X, offering instructions to his followers. Over the past several weeks, parallel scenarios have played out across X, Instagram, and Facebook, with users sharing tips on how to automate their unfollows with the help of Muse.

X user @justdrmj posted about the trend the same week as Roberts, and nearly every reply shared a taste for trivial grudge-holding. For him it came down to one simple rule: “Why be a fan?” “i agree. reciprocity is key,” one person said in response. “The way I just cleaned house,” added another. In a seeming outburst of celebration, one X user posted: “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG.”

Even tech worker Kimberly Munoz, who has 33,200 Instagram followers, said she wasn’t about to be “anybody’s fan,” noting in an Instagram video that she used the feature to suss out “people that I know in real life that have unfollowed me.” “I downloaded Muse just to do this only,” one person responded.

With social media rapidly evolving, there is no longer a unified consensus around etiquette. For some people, following others is an indication of friendship or simply a way to keep tabs on your latest crush. Others view it as more of a social obligation—you follow someone if they follow you, but the opposite is true as well.

Natalie Pennington, an associate professor who researches social connection at Colorado State University, wonders about the consequences of people gradually outsourcing small social decisions to technology.

“It is probably at least partially a question of not wanting to deal with emotionally uncomfortable things,” Pennington says. “This also strikes me as another example of information we don’t really need that social media can give us. There’s this data that exists at the platform level or would take a lot of effort to find out on your own, but now you can learn with the click of the button. But it doesn’t mean it is something you need to know.”

In October, despite the seeming popularity of the feature, Meta removed an advertising campaign that promoted Muse with the promise that users could “see who unfollowed you each week,” Business Insider reported.
When WIRED asked about the reasoning behind Meta’s decision to remove the ad, the company did not respond to a request for comment.
But Muse’s capabilities aren’t just being employed to even scores. Some people are using the assistant to streamline feeds that have become extremely cluttered over the years.

Elizabeth Brooks is a self-proclaimed “sweeper”—the term for a hobbyist who routinely enters sweepstakes and promotional contests—who, over the course of 10 years, had followed various accounts offering giveaways. Recently, she started prompting the assistant to bring her five profile links every few hours, no more than six times a day, for her to manually unfollow one by one. “Your following list can finally work for you instead of the other way around,” she wrote on Facebook.

Roberts, who joined Instagram in high school 15 years ago and calls the platform “my app of choice,” says people are becoming more intentional about their digital relationships and who they let into their online lives. But he doesn’t plan on letting Muse make any more decisions about his social life, he says.
“Unfollowing is where I draw the line.”

paragraphs: AI-translated article with transliterated names. Read original Chinese article here.

China’s securities regulator has told some law firms it will not approve plans by red-chip companies to list outside mainland China, people familiar with the matter said. The move marks a further tightening of China’s controls on offshore fundraising and will deal a blow to Hong Kong’s initial public offering (IPO) market.
Red-chip companies are incorporated outside China and legally classified as foreign companies, but hold assets and operate businesses within China through equity holdings or contractual arrangements.

Reuters reported on Friday (20 November), citing people familiar with the matter, that the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) recently told representatives of law firms that red-chip companies established after new offshore listing rules took effect in 2023 must move their place of incorporation back to China before they can list.

In March 2023, the CSRC introduced new filing rules for overseas securities offerings and listings by domestic companies, bringing both direct and indirect overseas listings under a filing-based regulatory framework.
Before that, Chinese companies did not need regulatory approval to raise funds overseas through offshore holding structures.
In March this year, the CSRC told Reuters it was reviewing the “necessity and compliance” of red-chip structures.

However, despite warnings from the authorities, some red-chip companies seeking IPOs and their advisers continued to seek regulatory approval, hoping to list outside mainland China without dismantling their existing structures or moving their place of incorporation back to China, according to one of the people familiar with the matter.
The person added that most applicants had failed to convince Chinese regulators that their red-chip structures were necessary, prompting the regulators to take a tougher stance.
This is an AI-translated article and some names may be transliterated. The original Chinese text remains authoritative, and SPH Media is not responsible for translation errors.

Secure messaging service Signal said it will restrict the screenshot function on smartphones to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations. In a blog post published on the 20th (local time), Signal pointed out that AI features built directly into operating systems (OS) are accessing device data in ways app developers cannot control, and demanded that platform operators such as Apple, Google and Microsoft provide concrete blocking tools.

news.summary_en: Signal has introduced default screenshot restrictions to prevent OS-level AI agents, such as Apple Siri and Google Gemini, from scraping screen data and bypassing end-to-end encryption. The company stated that these agents pose a severe privacy threat by leveraging system-level permissions and has urged Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide more granular platform control tools.
paragraphs: Secure messaging service Signal said it will restrict the screenshot function on smartphones to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations. In a blog post published on the 20th (local time), Signal pointed out that AI features built directly into operating systems (OS) are accessing device data in ways app developers cannot control, and demanded that platform operators such as Apple, Google and Microsoft provide concrete blocking tools.

Signal itself acknowledged that the measure is not complete. "The current wave of agentic AI integration is creating an environment that is increasingly hostile to privacy," the company said, calling it "an existential threat to Signal and our ability to uphold our mission." It added that "operating systems govern the very environment in which apps like Signal must exist."

The biggest concern is AI that is deeply integrated into the OS, such as Apple's Siri AI or Google's Gemini Intelligence. According to Signal, these agents can read what is displayed on screen and act on the user's behalf based on that, meaning that Signal messages protected by end-to-end encryption can be pulled outside the encrypted environment. The company noted that the moment AI scans the screen, Signal's security environment is neutralized.

With this measure, Signal will introduce a setting that blocks screenshot access on users' devices and turn it on by default. When Signal detects a screenshot attempt or an AI assistant's screen access, it displays a pop-up window that lets users lift the block depending on the device type. Signal also blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. However, it said such protections are difficult to provide reliably on Apple's macOS.

Signal's concerns are backed by a recently confirmed real-world case. It was confirmed that Meta's AI agent Muse bypassed official integration tools to access Signal messages on Apple computers and Google Android smartphones. Muse used the broad OS-level permissions granted during the app's initial setup to pull messages in ways users did not expect. On Apple's macOS, it combined accessibility tools with the screenshot function to capture Signal conversations, extract text from the images and reproduce it inside the Muse app.

Meta countered that an agent must be able to see and interact with the computer to act on the user's behalf, and that Muse accesses other apps only through permissions the user has explicitly granted. Apple blocked that path with an OS update released this week, but at the same time introduced a new permission system aimed at agents that allows similar functions with additional warnings.

Signal urged that app developers be given a clear way to fully exclude their apps from AI assistants' data processing, including screen reading, notifications and file system access. Signal, which is run by a nonprofit foundation, has minimized the data it stores on servers, excluded advertising and provided end-to-end encryption. The company's judgment is that these protections are neutralized the moment AI scans the screen.

The issue comes as Apple accelerates development of its own AI agent. In a recent job posting, Apple disclosed plans to develop a general-purpose AI agent that handles a computer like a human, performing web searches, coding, app control and coordination of multiple sub-agents. It is considering a launch as early as the end of next year, but development is still at an early stage. Apple CEO John Ternus is said to have urged Craig Federighi, senior vice president of software engineering, to push the AI strategy faster and more boldly.

The competitive landscape is also heating up quickly. Meta's Muse ranked second among free apps on Apple's App Store with restaurant and travel booking and news briefing features, while OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude also placed in the top five. Anthropic has expanded user testing of its own agent Duet, OpenAI has added features to Dots, and Google overhauled its agent tasks this week. After news of Apple's AI agent development emerged, Meta shares fell about 2% and Anthropic more than 3% in after-hours trading.

The market expects tensions between platform operators and privacy apps to intensify further. The fact that platforms can control the paths through which OS-integrated AI accesses other apps' data shows that competitiveness in the AI agent era depends not only on model performance but also on the design of access permissions at the operating system level. Apple has already been sued by the US Department of Justice, including over allegations that it blocked rivals' access to features and hardware, so attention is focused on how Signal's demands will be reflected. Signal assessed that in Apple's upcoming iOS 27.3, Siri will be able to call a car or book a restaurant through external apps, but that this is far from a full agent that moves across multiple apps and handles complex tasks on its own.
