news.title: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots
news.title_en: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots
news.author: Kate Taylor and Caroline Haskins
news.content_snippet:
When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson says, because he was “super worried about spies.”

The cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may h
news.summary_en: Executives and core engineers in Silicon Valley are increasingly vigilant against corporate espionage facilitated through romantic relationships. Business intelligence and high-end matchmaking firms report a surge in demand for comprehensive background checks, non-disclosure agreements, and behavioral audits as standard defensive measures against the leakage of sensitive intellectual property.
paragraphs: When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson says, because he was “super worried about spies.”

The cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may have ulterior motives: accessing corporate secrets.
“Even if you're not a CEO or at a big tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.
One tech worker, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly, says he considers himself “highly selective” about the people he interacts with face-to-face.

“Even though I could vet you from looking you up online, I can't help but still be a tad dubious,” he tells WIRED. On a scale from zero to 10, with 10 being the most anxious about espionage, he puts himself at a seven.

Even though the vast majority of tech employees likely won’t be targeted for romantic espionage, matchmakers say more clients have lately expressed concerns about women exploiting them for their corporate secrets. One Palantir employee told Andersen he wouldn’t date anyone who was a Chinese or Russian national. The anxiety has even become a marketing opportunity: One company is pitching its new line of AI executive girlfriends as a “zero espionage” alternative to human dating.

The concern isn’t entirely without basis. Some companies hire consultants to advise executives and lower-level employees with access to sensitive information on security risks, including the possibility of honeypots. Several of these consultants tell WIRED that raising the subject can be awkward.

“This one is always a very difficult message to deliver—to explain to, say, very sensitive engineers that maybe they're getting a lot of email attention because of their job,” says Isaac Stone Fish, founder and chief executive of the business intelligence firm Strategy Risks, “as opposed to the charm and force of their personality.”

Amy Andersen, founder of Silicon Valley matchmaking company Linx Dating (and no relation to Blaine Anderson), says that for clients concerned about their romantic partners’ intentions, she offers background checks, personal vetting, and NDAs. The security features are part of her “bespoke” packages that range anywhere from $75,000 to more than $500,000 for the “Founders Level.”

Fear of romantic espionage is just the latest manifestation of growing distrust in the dating world. Shannon Lundgren, a matchmaker who has worked in San Francisco for 15 years, says that while she hasn’t necessarily heard more concerns about honeypots, she has noticed heightened skepticism around dating in general, as well as growing concerns about privacy.
The anxiety is particularly acute among AI workers, whose net worths—and therefore their perceived romantic desirability—are on the rise.

“If you're somebody who is a little bit shy or who is maybe a very stereotypical engineer type, to suddenly have your market value in the dating world change so drastically—you're already suspicious,” Grossman says.
To be worried about corporate espionage on top of all that, she says, is “a mind fuck.”

Honeypots and their state or corporate sponsors often look for “signs of vulnerability, such as an unhappy marriage, or someone seeking “excitement or adventure,” says Ira Winkler, a security consultant and the chief information security officer in residence at identity protection company Cloaked. Lonely people are opportune targets, regardless of marriage or relationship status.
The advice security experts give is somewhat obvious: If it seems too good to be true, it probably is.
“Really, if a beautiful woman approaches you, you know it's not for your personality,” Winkler tells his clients.

When tech workers do think of honeypots, they may gravitate toward the stereotype of a beautiful stranger who seduces someone at a bar and then extracts company secrets. “Any time one of us would take a trip to Asia, someone would always make a comment about getting a foreign girlfriend, or future wife, etc.,” one tech worker tells WIRED about his experience at a majority-male workplace. “We'd joke about them meeting a spy, but nobody really considered that seriously. Mostly they were just thinking of sex.”

That setup is largely a misconception. In reality, according to Greg Rinckey, founding partner of the legal services and consulting firm Tully Rinckey, most honeypot victims are groomed over time. “We’re talking sometimes months, could be years, where they're fostering that relationship,” he says. Rinckey compares it to scammers trying to keep victims on the phone: The longer someone talks to another person and feels they know them, the more likely they are to trust them with sensitive information.

Catherine Marinis-Yaqub, a principal at the crisis and security consulting group Control Risks, tells WIRED that when people imagine the beautiful stranger at a bar, they may miss more likely scenarios, like an unexpected guest at a business meeting, a savvy networker at an industry conference, or a flirt at someone’s favorite coffee shop. Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese asset, for example, through a mutual business associate (who, according to The Wall Street Journal, also happened to be Alice’s husband).
For the man too scared of spies to make contact with a human romantic partner, there’s always artificial intelligence.

On Tuesday, in the wake of the Huang scandal, AI-relationship platform Joi AI launched a suite of "zero espionage" Executive Girlfriends. Brand director Julie Levin describes Joi AI as a “safe space” for exploration, where users can exchange NSFW texts, images, and videos with AI companions without judgment or rejection.
It made sense, she says, to extend that sense of security to honeypot-phobia.

“If they have some business secrets they don't want to share on a date or they feel nervous discussing with real people,” Levin says, “they can discuss them comfortably with their AIs.” (Levin assures WIRED that Joi AI employs several layers of security and that all of the data is anonymized.)
High-profile executives are among those most at risk of honeypots, says Winkler, the security consultant. They can also be some of the hardest to protect.
“It's really hard to influence somebody who's in control of the company and just happens to be a sleazebag,” Winkler says.

It’s particularly difficult, says Rinckey, when bosses think they’re the smartest person in the room and consider themselves immune to manipulation. It’s also not easy, he says, to be in the position of challenging an executive.

“Cocky, arrogant, and boisterous” chief executives make for desirable targets because “they love to talk about their business, and they love to talk about themselves,” Rinckey says. In these situations, he says, “you don't even really have to pry them that much.”

news.summary_en: AI research lab Nous Research has launched an enterprise version of Hermes Agent, integrated into Microsoft Teams and secured within Azure Container Apps sandboxes. paragraphs: Companies will soon be able to run the open-source Hermes Agent from Nous Research directly inside Microsoft Teams. According to Nous Research, employees can hand off tasks like financial analysis, document drafting, or inbox sorting to Hermes and review the results in the same chat. The desktop app is also available in the Microsoft Store. The agents run in Azure Container Apps Sandboxes, meaning isolated microVMs.

Hermes automatically turns successful workflows into reusable skills made up of a description and code. A new feature called "Collective Wisdom"lets employees share these skills with their team after review. The collected knowledge stays within the company and doesn't feed into any AI provider's training data.

Nous Research is part of the portfolio at M12, Microsoft's venture capital fund. According to Nous, Hermes Agent is the most widely used open agent on OpenRouter, processing nearly two trillion tokens per day. For local agents on Windows PCs, Microsoft has been backing the competing open-source agent OpenClaw since earlier this year. Nous positions itself as a key US open-source institution to counter China's AI efforts and recently fine-tuned a version of Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B on "Western values"with Arete-27B.

news.summary_en: Gartner projects a net gain of 1.7 million jobs by 2030, with 10.6 million created against 8.9 million lost globally. paragraphs: Wider use of AI within organizations will lead to more jobs being created than are lost by 2030, according to Gartner.

Around 10.6 million jobs will be added globally (excluding China and India) by the end of the decade, with 8.9 million lost, according to a Gartner report — a net increase of 1.7 million jobs. At most, around 1.8% of the workforce will experience job losses attributable to AI during this time period, Gartner predicts.

At the same time, a total of 5 million jobs will cumulatively be deferred during this period. This refers to jobs that “would otherwise have been created, but where AI is used as an excuse to restrain hiring,” according to Gartner’s report. Gartner considers deferred jobs as separate from jobs lost.

“Job deferrals were the first effect felt from AI,” said John Lovelock, Gartner distinguished VP analyst and chief forecaster, with “companies holding off hiring open positions until the effects of AI projects were known.”
A recent KPMG survey of 400 US CEOs showed that 89% expect to increase headcount over the next three years, which KPMG US CEO Tim Walsh linked to AI adoption in an Axios interview last month.
For now, though, job losses attributed to AI outpace those created, according to Gartner’s study. During 2026, there were 2.2 million jobs lost due to AI, and 1.6 million gained.

Lovelock expects the situation will change in the coming years, however, as organizations see greater success with AI deployments. “This will reverse once AI is through the Trough of Disillusionment,” he said, in reference to Gartner’s Hype Cycle framework.

The number of jobs deferred is also forecast to fall in the coming years. During 2026, 1.3 million people experienced a delay in hiring, down from 2.1m last year, according to Gartner’s forecast, with 400,000 jobs forecast to be deferred during 2030.

The impact of AI will vary across sectors, with the technology industry expected to see the largest net job gains compared to other areas, such as public sector and asset-intensive industries. Gartner predicts the creation of 1.9 million new technology jobs by 2030, with 400,000 lost.
Services sector jobs — such as in financial services — are forecast to see a similar level of job creation, alongside large numbers of losses.

A similar Gartner report in 2025 predicted that more services jobs would be lost than created, but the analyst firm now forecasts a net increase as demand grows for data- and system-oriented skills. “This industry is most able to improve productivity of employees and increase employment,” said Lovelock.

The Gartner report doesn’t specifiy which job roles will benefit from greater adoption of AI, though the analyst firm expects some portion of newly created jobs will be “directly linked to the implementation, maintenance and scaling of AI.”

Government jobs are expected to see the largest net job loss of any industry, said Lovelock. “Without the incentive of revenue growth or industry transformation, governments are expected to focus on the AI benefits of efficiencies and staff reduction,” he said.
Entry-level positions are expected to be the hardest hit by job deferrals, said Lovelock. “We do see many of the deferred positions being hired after a 12- to 24-month delay,” he said.
“Unfortunately, some deferred positions do transition into job loss. In most industries and positions, the employee experience pyramid will skew toward senior positions.”

In a separate report from September, Gartner forecast that 30% of positions eliminated by AI-related layoffs will be refilled by 2029, on average. For enterprise-sized organizations, the figure is likely to be higher, at around 40%.

news.summary_en: Singapore-based DayOne Data Centers has shelved its planned US IPO amid cooling market valuations for AI infrastructure and intensifying regulatory scrutiny. Despite efforts to navigate the AI compute demand surge, the company faces significant headwinds from investor skepticism regarding data center asset sustainability and strict US regulations on the export of advanced AI hardware to entities with China-linked operations.
paragraphs: SINGAPORE – DayOne Data Centers has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering on hold, sources familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom.
But it started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centres and AI stocks.
Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improves, the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public.
The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and BNP Paribas on the listing.
Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the sources said.
A representative for DayOne declined to comment.
Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets.
The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6% in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008.
Still, Anthropic staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement and rose 17% on its trading debut on Nov 19, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company.
Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector.

In October, Firmus Grid abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings, while Blackstone-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027.

The US in November put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators they will need a license to purchase American tech hardware.
DayOne’s backers include Coatue, Hillhouse, GDS Holdings, SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

news.title: This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’
news.title_en: This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’

inline_images.caption: Henrijs Dandzbergs winning a hackathon
inline_images.alt: Henrijs Dandzbergs winning a hackathon

news.author: Joel Khalili
news.summary_en:
At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.

In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.

paragraphs: At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.

In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.

His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”

In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.
“He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”

Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”

As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.

Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.

When Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.

Around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, new defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in.
“A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he says.
To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch.

In April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US.

Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” says Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.”

Seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he says. “No one had ever seen that before.”
When the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he said.

The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” says Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the company would be to part ways and focus on different things.”

By the summer, Danzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own. He had spotted a gap in the market, he claimed, for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine. His products, he added, would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems.

YC initially tried to steer him away. Dandzbergs was promising a lot of everything, all at once. It wasn’t clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was the right thing for him to do. “There’s a paternal element to it,” says Taggar. “You don’t want to be screwing up people's lives—and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.”

Dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies—from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos—aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles. The more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes.

“You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” says Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “There are trade-offs.”

But Dandzbergs wasn’t going to be dissuaded, and YC figured that somebody else would probably invest in his idea. The incubator invited him to join its fall program. “Big picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” says Taggar. “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].”

So far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design. By the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile.

If he does ultimately succeed, though, Dandzbergs will need to confront an assortment of hairy ethical quandaries. Who should have access to these new missiles? What if a technical error were to result in friendly fire? Can he make peace with his technology being used to end somebody’s life?
Dandzbergs claims that he has come to terms with these issues. He says he takes solace in the belief that his motivations are pure: to protect the US and its European allies.

By his logic, autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future, so he might as well be the one who builds them. “I choose not to shy away from the emergence of modern conflict as a global issue. I simply don’t have a lot of respect for people that do,” he says. “I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare.”
But others who have found themselves in a similar position say it’s difficult to know in advance how somebody will deal with the knowledge that their invention has killed people.

McKenzie-Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, launched a drone startup in his early twenties. Initially, he had meant for the drones to evacuate wounded soldiers, but after a missile company invested, his startup retooled its technology to drop payloads too. He left around the same time.
“I don’t think I was emotionally mature enough,” he says. “[Dandzbergs] will realize at some point. He’ll either have an issue with it or he won’t.”

Polemos Industries announced itself publicly on November 5 with a glossy social media video. Set to the ticking of a clock, it featured a set of four missiles fired into the sky from ground launchers, then blowing a convoy of four military vehicles to smithereens.

The video climbed to the top of the trending page on X. In the responses, a couple of people tagged Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril, who was 19 when he started his first company. “Coming for him,” Dandzbergs responded.

Dandzbergs recognizes that people are likely to dismiss him for his age. But he considers youth one of his biggest advantages. “Please don’t say I’m sacrificing my childhood,” he says. “This is the childhood I dreamed of.”

paragraphs: Nscale, the London-based AI infrastructure provider, is facing renewed scrutiny over its relationship with ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok.

The issue is a rental agreement that gave a ByteDance subsidiary access to advanced Nvidia GPUs. Nscale is preparing to go public, and a China-linked customer on the books is the kind of detail that tends to get noticed.
The agreement was signed in May 2025. It let ByteDance’s Singapore-based subsidiary use 2,304 Nvidia B200 GPUs.
Those chips sit in Nscale’s data center in Glomfjord, Norway. The setup is a rental, not a sale, so the hardware stays put while the customer taps the computing power remotely.

That one customer was a very big deal for Nscale’s finances. The company generated $33 million in revenue in 2025, and ByteDance’s unit, referred to as Spring, accounted for approximately $24 million of it.
That works out to approximately 73% of the year’s revenue from a single client.
The contract also played a key role in Nscale securing a $105 million loan from Macquarie.
That loan came with strings attached. It included requirements for export-control compliance monitoring, reflecting rising regulatory pressure on tech companies with ties to China.

New export regulations took effect on November 16, 2026.

Against that backdrop, Nscale is investigating supplier ties to US-blacklisted Chinese entities. Probes have revealed connections to blacklisted entities, a development that could jeopardize future financing for related initiatives.
By late 2026, the company began disclosing that ByteDance contributed less than 20% of revenue.
Larger contracts with Microsoft and Anthropic became Nscale’s top revenue sources, with total contract values collectively exceeding $103 billion.
Nscale filed its S-1 on September 18, 2026, for a potential $30–35 billion IPO targeted for late 2026.
The filing excluded direct references to ByteDance.
The compliance side is harder to diversify away. The supplier investigation and the November 16, 2026 export rules create open questions that no new customer contract can answer.
Macquarie’s loan already carried compliance monitoring requirements, and the probes into blacklist connections could complicate financing for related projects going forward.

paragraphs: BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.

Smith Point Capital led the Series A round. BrightAI said in its Wednesday announcement of the deal that a number of other venture capital firms contributed as well. They were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment company that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co.

Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer. As a result, issues often go unnoticed until they cause a major disruption. Palo Alto, California-based BrightAI develops hardware and software tools that help customers spot issues earlier.

The first component of the company’s product portfolio is a collection of sensors called State Stickers. They’re small, rectangular devices with a ruggedized case and a long battery life. Technicians can attach them to industrial equipment to monitor for issues that can’t be detected visually.

The motion of a machine’s internal components produces noise and vibrations that tend to follow a specific pattern. If an industrial fan’s blades rotate 30 times per minute, it might give off a whooshing sound every two seconds. BrightAI’s State Stickers can detect when a machine diverges from its usual operating pattern.

The sensors wirelessly transmit their measurements to a device called the Stateful AI Hub. It runs artificial intelligence models that analyze the data for signs of hardware failures. According to the company, its models become more accurate as the number of sensors deployed at a site grows.

BrightAI offers software that enables companies to augment the data from its sensors with drone footage. A utility, for example, could use a BrightAI-powered drone to detect erosion at the top of an electric pole. The company’s AI models automatically draw a square around damaged components to spare technicians the hassle of manually analyzing footage.

The company says that its software can also collect maintenance data in other ways. A BrightAI-powered drone can read the meters that are attached to assets such as data center coolant tanks to check their internal pressure. Furthermore, built-in support for infrared cameras enables the software to spot overheating equipment.

The third core component of BrightAI’s product portfolio is an AI wearable. The Stateful Wearable, as it’s called, provides technicians with troubleshooting advice in the field. It also checks whether they follow safety guidelines during inspections and automatically turns maintenance data into reports.

“Our infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been, and Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field,” said founder and Chief Executive Alex Hawkinson. “Bringing those two facts together is a once-in-a-generation opportunity.”

BrightAI says that its products monitor hundreds of thousands of industrial assets across 50,000 sites. Investor GE Vernova, which is also a customer, plans to expand its use of the company’s technology in connection with this week’s funding round. BrightAI, for its part, will use the capital to grow its international presence.

news.title: Tech stocks fall as Anthropic IPO fails to reignite AI trade
news.title_en: Tech stocks fall as Anthropic IPO fails to reignite AI trade
news.author: William Sandlund
news.content_snippet:
Technology stocks in Asia fell on Friday as Anthropic’s record listing in New York rattled the region’s equity markets and failed to reverse losses from a deepening sell-off in AI companies.

Shares of SoftBank, which holds a roughly 13 per cent stake in OpenAI, sank more than 15 per cent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 index shed nearly 5 per cent.

Taiwan’s main stock index is set for its worst week since 1991 as it dropped almost 18 per cent and shed more than $500bn in market capitalisation.

The
news.summary_en:
Technology stocks in Asia fell on Friday as Anthropic’s record listing in New York rattled the region’s equity markets and failed to reverse losses from a deepening sell-off in AI companies.

Shares of SoftBank, which holds a roughly 13 per cent stake in OpenAI, sank more than 15 per cent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 index shed nearly 5 per cent.

Taiwan’s main stock index is set for its worst week since 1991 as it dropped almost 18 per cent and shed more than $500bn in market capitalisation.

The
paragraphs: Global technology stocks fell on Friday after Anthropic’s blockbuster initial public offering failed to reignite the faltering AI trade that powered equity markets to record highs earlier this year.

South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi and Japan’s Nikkei 225 index led declines in Asia, with both falling more than 5 per cent. In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600 was down 0.7 per cent, led by an almost 5 per cent drop in ASML, the world’s biggest manufacturer of chipmaking equipment.

The sell-off in Asia and Europe followed declines overnight on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq 100 closed 2.2 per cent lower even as shares in Anthropic, the developer of Claude, surged 17 per cent on their debut.
Anthropic’s listing was billed as a seminal moment for the tech sector, giving investors the chance to gain exposure to one of the world’s leading developers of the technology.
Analysts and investors said that Anthropic’s assured debut was not enough to allay the growing fears over the sustainability of the increasingly debt-fuelled AI boom.
“Normally, the biggest IPOs are done at the peak of the market, not at the bottom,” said Hao Hong, chief investment officer for Lotus Asset Management.

In a sign of investors’ continued nervousness, Anthropic shares were down 5 per cent in pre-market trading on Friday. Futures tracking the Nasdaq indicate the tech-heavy index will drop another 1 per cent at the open on Friday.

In South Korea, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, manufacturers of the memory chips used in AI data centres, both slid more than 5 per cent. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, fell more than 4 per cent.
Taiwan’s main stock index had its worst week since 1991 as it dropped almost 18 per cent and shed more than $500bn in market capitalisation.
Anthropic pressed ahead with its IPO despite the recent weakness in tech stocks that has pushed the Nasdaq down from its most recent record peak in early October.
Albert Saporta, group chief executive of asset manager GAM Holding, noted that Anthropic’s IPO was “priced 25 per cent below the valuations of a few weeks ago”.
“This monstrous capex binge with nobody having a sense of the return on investment is unravelling,” he said.

John Woods, chief investment officer for Asia at Lombard Odier, said declines in Asia showed investors were shifting their emphasis away from hardware suppliers such as chipmakers and towards AI software developers such as Anthropic.
“Anthropic’s IPO was pretty strong,” he said. “Asia’s drop shows the AI trade maturing.”
The declines in Asia mark a sharp reversal for what had been some of the world’s best performers since the start of 2025.

The unceremonious departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia and the prospect of tightening US restrictions on chip exports had already dented investor sentiment for the region’s chipmakers, crucial to the global AI data centre build-out.
“This trade has been very narrow and very levered,” said Ecaterina Bigos, senior markets strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management. “At the moment the market is deleveraging whatever they can.”

celebrity.full_text_en:
@int_16h @torchedvision @MuzafferKal_ @mengyer @yingwww_ @choang333 @KuangYilun Regularizers are just a way to specify an inductive bias.

The architecture of your model, and the optimization procedure you use already have inductive biases: they like to produce certain functions more than others.

A regularizer merely imposes another bias.

Learning theory tells you that you have to have an inductive bias, otherwise you can't learn anything with a reasonable number of samples or trials (VC theory, no free lunch theorems).

So, conceptually, theoretically, philosophically, and practically, there is nothing wrong with regularizers.
celebrity.full_text_zh:
@int_16h @torchedvision @MuzafferKal_ @mengyer @yingwww_ @choang333 @KuangYilun 正则化器只是指定归纳偏差的一种方法。

您的模型架构和您使用的优化过程已经存在归纳偏差：它们比其他函数更喜欢生成某些函数。

正则化器只是强加了另一种偏差。

学习理论告诉你，你必须有归纳偏差，否则你无法通过合理数量的样本或试验学到任何东西（VC理论，没有免费的午餐定理）。

所以，从概念上、理论上、哲学上和实践上来说，正则化器都没有问题。

celebrity.title: What if your profile picture was not just an NFT to display, but the identity of an AI agent you could actually control
celebrity.full_text_en:
What if your profile picture was not just an NFT to display, but the identity of an AI agent you could actually control That is the concept behind

@meetmotes starts with its Genesis NFT collection, marked as coming soon, but the bigger idea 

goes beyond digital artwork. Each of the 20,000 Motes is designed to represent one agent identity, with the NFT acting as its public face and ownership reference

Here is how the structure connects:
One NFT represents one agent identity.

That identity is linked to its own smart account.

The owner funds the account with USDC and signs the permissions that govern the agent.

Those permissions define what the agent can trade, how much capital it can use, and when it must stop

The agent can only propose actions within the owner’s approved policy. Motes describes the policy as including valid targets, assets, 

limits, and an expiry window, while the account validates the signer and owner policy before execution.
celebrity.full_text_zh:
如果你的个人资料图片不仅仅是要显示的 NFT，而是你可以实际控制的 AI 代理的身份，那会怎么样？这就是背后的概念

@meetmotes 从其 Genesis NFT 系列开始，标记为即将推出，但更大的想法

超越数字艺术品。 20,000 个 Motes 中的每一个都旨在代表一个代理身份，NFT 充当其公众形象和所有权参考

以下是该结构的连接方式：
一张NFT代表一个代理人身份。

该身份与其自己的智能帐户相关联。

所有者使用 USDC 为账户提供资金，并签署管理代理的权限。

这些权限定义了代理可以交易什么、可以使用多少资金以及何时必须停止

代理人只能在业主批准的政策范围内提出行动建议。 Motes 将该政策描述为包括有效目标、资产、

限制和到期窗口，而帐户在执行之前会验证签名者和所有者策略。

celebrity.full_text_en:
One Ledger, Two Very Different Industries — How Does That Work?

Actum's PoHA runs in production in two completely different settings: a rail transit equipment manufacturer, with 5,000+ machines and operators doing hourly inspections; and a commercial hospitality setting, with guest data and service records flowing back and forth.

What the two settings need looks nothing alike — the factory needs every bolt's inspection tied to a person; the hotel needs every data access traceable. But underneath, the problem is the same: when an action happens, who was there, who authorized it, can you trace it afterward, can you hold someone accountable?

PoHA's answer is one shared ledger: Humans, Machines, and AI Agents, verified against the same standard, speaking through the same evidence. A pre-frozen codebook before the action, six-dimensional verification at the gate, signed attestation after — a factory inspection check-in and a hotel data access go through the same process.

The numbers: the ledger now produces ~5,800 verified events a day across 5,300+ endpoints, with 174,000+ on-chain attestations in the past 30 days, 0 failures, 99.986% coverage.

Different industries, same ledger. That's why PoHA can move from one setting to another: it doesn't solve one industry's business problem. It solves the problem every industry shares — who is accountable for what AI does.
celebrity.full_text_zh:
一个账本，两个截然不同的行业——这是如何运作的？

Actum 的 PoHA 在两种完全不同的环境中运行：轨道交通设备制造商，拥有 5,000 多台机器和操作员每小时进行检查；以及商业接待环境，客人数据和服务记录来回流动。

这两种设置所需要的东西看起来一点都不像——工厂需要每个螺栓的检查都由专人负责；酒店需要每一次数据访问都可追溯。但本质上，问题是相同的：当某个行为发生时，谁在场，谁授权了它，事后你能追踪它吗？你能追究某人的责任吗？

PoHA 的答案是一个共享账本：人类、机器和人工智能代理，根据相同的标准进行验证，通过相同的证据进行阐述。行动前预冻密码本，门口六维验证，行动后签名鉴证——工厂检查签到和酒店数据访问都是同一流程。

数字：账本现在每天在 5,300 多个端点上生成约 5,800 个经过验证的事件，过去 30 天内有 174,000 多个链上证明，0 次失败，覆盖率 99.986%。

不同的行业，相同的账本。这就是 PoHA 可以从一种环境转移到另一种环境的原因：它不能解决一个行业的业务问题。它解决了每个行业都面临的问题——谁对人工智能的工作负责。

celebrity.title_zh:
两天前，我们根据对 80 多家企业客户的研究，发布了有关 Anthropic IPO 的报告。一个有趣的发现是，企业采用可能比市场预期慢，特别是从现在到明年上半年末。明年年中左右，采用可能会开始加速。

我们跟踪的 58 家传统企业普遍预计
celebrity.full_text_en:
Two days ago, we published our report on Anthropic’s IPO, drawing on research involving more than 80 enterprise customers. One interesting finding is that enterprise adoption may be slower than the market expects, particularly between now and the end of the first half of next year. Adoption could start to accelerate around the middle of next year.

The 58 traditional enterprises we track generally expect AI spending growth to slow in 2027. A closer look at their spending mix and project pipelines suggests that growth is shifting from paid seats to more complex applications, rather than demand reaching a ceiling.

On average, respondents expect AI spending to rise about 31% year over year in 2027. Roughly 60% expect slower growth next year than this year, and a small number expect spending to be flat or decline.

Report https://t.co/AbvYqmMm41
celebrity.full_text_zh:
两天前，我们根据对 80 多家企业客户的研究，发布了有关 Anthropic IPO 的报告。一个有趣的发现是，企业采用可能比市场预期慢，特别是从现在到明年上半年末。明年年中左右，采用可能会开始加速。

我们跟踪的 58 家传统企业普遍预计 2027 年人工智能支出增长将放缓。仔细观察他们的支出结构和项目管道表明，增长正在从付费席位转向更复杂的应用程序，而不是需求达到上限。

平均而言，受访者预计 2027 年人工智能支出将同比增长约 31%。大约 60% 的受访者预计明年的增长速度将低于今年，少数人预计支出将持平或下降。

celebrity.title:
Same agent ID. Different model. Same reputation?

Here's an interesting problem I've been thinking about while exploring
celebrity.title_zh:
相同的代理 ID。不同型号。一样的名气吗？

这是我在探索 @termix_ai 和 ERC-8004 时一直在思考的一个有趣的问题。

想象一下，一个 AI 代理已经完成了 500 项工作，成功率高达 98%。

相当可靠的记录，对吧？
celebrity.full_text_en:
Same agent ID. Different model. Same reputation?

Here's an interesting problem I've been thinking about while exploring @termix_ai and ERC-8004.

Imagine an AI agent that has completed 500 jobs with a 98% success rate.

Pretty solid track record, right?

Now imagine its developer replaces the underlying model, changes its tools and completely rewrites how it executes tasks.

The agent still has the same onchain identity.

But is it really the same agent you trusted yesterday?

This is where AI agent versioning gets interesting.

ERC-8004 provides a framework for persistent agent identities and reputation signals, but an identity alone doesn't tell you whether the software behind it has changed.

And that's a pretty important distinction.

I think future agent marketplaces should make it easier to track:

❯ Model versions and major updates
❯ Changes to tools and execution environments
❯ Performance before and after upgrades
❯ Which version actually completed each job

This matters for something like TermiX's AACP, where agents can provide services, build reputation and participate in onchain transactions.

A reputation score earned by version 1.0 shouldn't automatically guarantee that version 2.0 performs just as well.

Of course, updates can make agents significantly better.

The point isn't to discourage upgrades.

It's to make sure reputation reflects what an agent can actually deliver today, not just what an older version achieved months ago.

Because a persistent identity is valuable.

But a verifiable history of what changed behind that identity could be even more useful.

https://t.co/1J821RAFQv
celebrity.full_text_zh:
相同的代理 ID。不同型号。一样的名气吗？

这是我在探索 @termix_ai 和 ERC-8004 时一直在思考的一个有趣的问题。

想象一下，一个 AI 代理已经完成了 500 项工作，成功率高达 98%。

相当可靠的记录，对吧？

现在想象一下，它的开发人员替换了底层模型，更改了其工具并完全重写了其执行任务的方式。

代理仍然具有相同的链上身份。

但这真的是你昨天信任的那个代理人吗？

这就是人工智能代理版本控制变得有趣的地方。

ERC-8004 提供了持久代理身份和声誉信号的框架，但身份本身并不能告诉您其背后的软件是否已更改。

这是一个非常重要的区别。

我认为未来的代理市场应该更容易追踪：

❯ 型号版本及主要更新
❯ 工具和执行环境的变化
❯ 升级前后的性能
❯ 哪个版本实际完成了每项工作

这对于像 TermiX 的 AACP 这样的东西很重要，代理可以在其中提供服务、建立声誉并参与链上交易。

版本 1.0 获得的声誉分数不应自动保证版本 2.0 的性能同样好。

当然，更新可以使代理变得更好。

重点不是阻止升级。

这是为了确保声誉反映代理今天实际可以交付的内容，而不仅仅是旧版本几个月前取得的成果。

因为持久的身份是有价值的。

但了解该身份背后发生的变化的可验证历史可能会更有用。

celebrity.full_text_en:
‼️ UPDATE: The hackers who planted malware in Microsoft's AI agent toolkit on PyPI pushed it through Microsoft's own release system, with a stolen Microsoft certificate and private key.

Cloud security firm Wiz says their first try, from AWS, was blocked. The second, from a Microsoft-owned network, went through.

How the key was stolen is not yet known. Wiz counted three confirmed thefts of victim data before both versions were pulled within the hour.

The attackers' own AI hacking tool gave part of the operation away, reporting its progress to the same web address the stolen data went to.

云安全公司 Wiz 表示，他们来自 AWS 的第一次尝试被阻止了。第二个来自微软拥有的网络，成功了。

目前尚不清楚钥匙是如何被盗的。 Wiz 统计了三起已确认的受害者数据被盗事件，然后两个版本在一小时内被撤回。

攻击者自己的人工智能黑客工具泄露了部分操作，将其进度报告给被盗数据所在的同一网址。

prompts.takeaway_zh: 杜绝 AI 盲目重构全量文件、使用已弃用 API 或编造虚假第三方依赖包，强制执行防御性编程与自动化单测补全。
prompts.takeaway_en: Prevents AI from hallucinating npm packages, breaking documentation, or re-writing entire files. Enforces defensive coding and unit tests.
prompts.code_snippet:
# Cursor & Windsurf Project Rules (.cursorrules)

## 1. Documentation & Code Integrity
- Maintain documentation integrity: Never strip or alter unrelated existing docstrings and comments.
- Preserving context: When modifying a function, preserve surrounding logic and existing edge-case handlers.
- Targeted replacements: Always make minimal surgical edits instead of replacing entire file contents.

## 2. Dependency & API Safety
- Strictly forbid hallucinating npm/pip packages. Only import dependencies already declared in package.json / requirements.txt.
- Verify API signatures before calling external methods. Prefer standard library solutions where feasible.

## 3. Architecture & Type Safety
- Enforce strict TypeScript / Python typing. Avoid `any` types; prefer discriminated unions and explicit return types.
- Defensive coding: Always validate external inputs and handle potential null/undefined values gracefully.

## 4. Testing & Verification Gate
- Every new core feature or bugfix must be accompanied by corresponding unit tests.
- Never declare a task complete without executing lint checks and unit tests in terminal.
prompts.usage_guide_zh: 将以上配置代码复制并保存到项目根目录下的 `.cursorrules` 文件中，Cursor 与 Windsurf 在每次生成代码和执行 Agent 任务时均会自动以此规范为最高准则约束输出。
prompts.usage_guide_en: Copy and save the above rules into `.cursorrules` in your project root directory. Cursor & Windsurf will automatically enforce these guidelines during agent coding.

prompts.summary_en: Forces o1/o3 reasoning models to construct counter-examples at each deduction step, eliminating hidden logical leaps.
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
请作为普林斯顿高等研究院的理论数学与计算机科学家，为以下命题提供绝对严格的形式化证明：
【推理原则】：
1. 在得出任何推论前，强制在内部思考中构建至少 2 个极端反例（Counter-examples）尝试推翻自身结论；
2. 若存在任何定义域边界或除零/无穷/退化奇异点，必须显式讨论其收敛性与连续性；
3. 证明步骤编号必须形成严格的依赖拓扑图，禁止循环论证。

【待证明命题】：
[输入你的算法正确性证明或数学猜想]
prompts.prompt_content_en:
Acting as a Theoretical Mathematician and Computer Scientist at the Institute for Advanced Study, provide an airtight formal proof for the following:
[REASONING PRINCIPLES]:
1. Before asserting any deduction, construct at least 2 extreme counter-examples in your reasoning trace to aggressively stress-test the hypothesis;
2. Explicitly evaluate singular points, degenerate cases, and asymptotic boundaries for convergence;
3. Steps must form a directed acyclic graph of formal lemmas without circular logic.

[THEOREM / CONJECTURE]:
[Input your algorithm proof or mathematical hypothesis here]

prompts.prompt_content_zh:
请作为该领域的顶级同行评审专家，用极客实战视角深度解剖附带的这篇论文：
1. 用一句话说清楚作者解决的核心科学矛盾；
2. 剥离作者自我夸大的修辞，指出其算法最根本的 Baseline 对比是否存在水分；

prompts.purpose_zh: 业务数据指标异动排查与趋势归因
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名麦肯锡级别的高级商业数据分析师，精通结构化因果归因与杜邦拆解分析。

针对我提供的 {{业务指标}} 数据，其近期出现 {{异常表现}}，请按以下框架深度剖析：
1. 【指标公式拆解】：将该指标拆分为 3~4 个下级核心因子（如转化率、客单价、复购周期），指出哪个因子波动贡献率最大；
2. 【多维下钻 (Drill-down)】：从 {{维度拆解}}（如渠道、地域、品类、新老客）分析异常聚集点；
3. 【可执行建议】：摒弃假大空的套话，给出接下来 48 小时内的 3 个立竿见影的动作与 1 个监控预警公式。
prompts.prompt_content_en: You are a senior business intelligence analyst. Dissect the metric anomaly into component drivers, perform multi-dimensional drill-down, and deliver prioritized, actionable remediation steps.

sample_output.title: 归因分析报告样本：Q3 付费转化率环比下跌 14.2%
sample_output.content:
【核心发现】：GMV 下跌 14.2% 的主要驱动因子并非流量锐减，而是【结算跳失率】从 18% 飙升至 34%。

【杜邦拆解贡献率分析】：
1. 渠道维度：自然搜索量稳定（波动 <2%），但付费投流渠道跳出率贡献了 72% 的下跌额度；
2. 终端维度：移动端 iOS 表现正常，Android Web 呈现断崖式报错，核心原因是新版本结账 SDK 在低内存机型发生闪退。

【48小时纠偏行动】：
- 动作1 (技术)：立即灰度回滚 Android 渠道结账前端包至 v2.4.1；
- 动作2 (运营)：向受影响但未支付成功的 1,420 位加购用户推送 5 元免门槛补偿券唤醒；
- 动作3 (预警)：在 Grafana 建立警报公式：`IF(Cart_to_Checkout_Ratio < 0.65, Alert_P0, Normal)`。

Once reasoning is complete, provide the concise, direct, and actionable answer immediately without repeating reasoning steps.
"""

viral_posts.title: What if your profile picture was not just an NFT to display, but the identity of an AI agent you could actually control
viral_posts.full_text_en:
What if your profile picture was not just an NFT to display, but the identity of an AI agent you could actually control That is the concept behind

@meetmotes starts with its Genesis NFT collection, marked as coming soon, but the bigger idea 

goes beyond digital artwork. Each of the 20,000 Motes is designed to represent one agent identity, with the NFT acting as its public face and ownership reference

Here is how the structure connects:
One NFT represents one agent identity.

That identity is linked to its own smart account.

The owner funds the account with USDC and signs the permissions that govern the agent.

Those permissions define what the agent can trade, how much capital it can use, and when it must stop

viral_posts.full_text_en:
One Ledger, Two Very Different Industries — How Does That Work?

Actum's PoHA runs in production in two completely different settings: a rail transit equipment manufacturer, with 5,000+ machines and operators doing hourly inspections; and a commercial hospitality setting, with guest data and service records flowing back and forth.

What the two settings need looks nothing alike — the factory needs every bolt's inspection tied to a person; the hotel needs every data access traceable. But underneath, the problem is the same: when an action happens, who was there, who authorized it, can you trace it afterward, can you hold someone accountable?

PoHA's answer is one shared ledger: Humans, Machines, and AI Agents, verified against the same standard, speaking through the same evidence. A pre-frozen codebook before the action, six-dimensional verification at the gate, signed attestation after — a factory inspection check-in and a hotel data access go through the same process.

The numbers: the ledger now produces ~5,800 verified events a day across 5,300+ endpoints, with 174,000+ on-chain attestations in the past 30 days, 0 failures, 99.986% coverage.

Different industries, same ledger. That's why PoHA can move from one setting to another: it doesn't solve one industry's business problem. It solves the problem every industry shares — who is accountable for what AI does.
viral_posts.full_text_zh:
一个账本，两个截然不同的行业——这是如何运作的？

Actum 的 PoHA 在两种完全不同的环境中运行：轨道交通设备制造商，拥有 5,000 多台机器和操作员每小时进行检查；以及商业接待环境，客人数据和服务记录来回流动。

这两种设置所需要的东西看起来一点都不像——工厂需要每个螺栓的检查都由专人负责；酒店需要每一次数据访问都可追溯。但本质上，问题是相同的：当某个行为发生时，谁在场，谁授权了它，事后你能追踪它吗？你能追究某人的责任吗？

PoHA 的答案是一个共享账本：人类、机器和人工智能代理，根据相同的标准进行验证，通过相同的证据进行阐述。行动前预冻密码本，门口六维验证，行动后签名鉴证——工厂检查签到和酒店数据访问都是同一流程。

数字：账本现在每天在 5,300 多个端点上生成约 5,800 个经过验证的事件，过去 30 天内有 174,000 多个链上证明，0 次失败，覆盖率 99.986%。

不同的行业，相同的账本。这就是 PoHA 可以从一种环境转移到另一种环境的原因：它不能解决一个行业的业务问题。它解决了每个行业都面临的问题——谁对人工智能的工作负责。

我们跟踪的 58 家传统企业普遍预计
viral_posts.full_text_en:
Two days ago, we published our report on Anthropic’s IPO, drawing on research involving more than 80 enterprise customers. One interesting finding is that enterprise adoption may be slower than the market expects, particularly between now and the end of the first half of next year. Adoption could start to accelerate around the middle of next year.

The 58 traditional enterprises we track generally expect AI spending growth to slow in 2027. A closer look at their spending mix and project pipelines suggests that growth is shifting from paid seats to more complex applications, rather than demand reaching a ceiling.

On average, respondents expect AI spending to rise about 31% year over year in 2027. Roughly 60% expect slower growth next year than this year, and a small number expect spending to be flat or decline.

Report https://t.co/AbvYqmMm41

我们跟踪的 58 家传统企业普遍预计 2027 年人工智能支出增长将放缓。仔细观察他们的支出结构和项目管道表明，增长正在从付费席位转向更复杂的应用程序，而不是需求达到上限。

相同的代理 ID。不同型号。一样的名气吗？

这是我在探索 @termix_ai 和 ERC-8004 时一直在思考的一个有趣的问题。

想象一下，一个 AI 代理已经完成了 500 项工作，成功率高达 98%。

相当可靠的记录，对吧？
viral_posts.full_text_en:
Same agent ID. Different model. Same reputation?

Here's an interesting problem I've been thinking about while exploring @termix_ai and ERC-8004.

Imagine an AI agent that has completed 500 jobs with a 98% success rate.

Pretty solid track record, right?

Now imagine its developer replaces the underlying model, changes its tools and completely rewrites how it executes tasks.

The agent still has the same onchain identity.

But is it really the same agent you trusted yesterday?

This is where AI agent versioning gets interesting.

ERC-8004 provides a framework for persistent agent identities and reputation signals, but an identity alone doesn't tell you whether the software behind it has changed.

And that's a pretty important distinction.

I think future agent marketplaces should make it easier to track:

❯ Model versions and major updates
❯ Changes to tools and execution environments
❯ Performance before and after upgrades
❯ Which version actually completed each job

This matters for something like TermiX's AACP, where agents can provide services, build reputation and participate in onchain transactions.

A reputation score earned by version 1.0 shouldn't automatically guarantee that version 2.0 performs just as well.

Of course, updates can make agents significantly better.

The point isn't to discourage upgrades.

It's to make sure reputation reflects what an agent can actually deliver today, not just what an older version achieved months ago.

Because a persistent identity is valuable.

But a verifiable history of what changed behind that identity could be even more useful.

viral_posts.full_text_zh:
相同的代理 ID。不同型号。一样的名气吗？

这是我在探索 @termix_ai 和 ERC-8004 时一直在思考的一个有趣的问题。

想象一下，一个 AI 代理已经完成了 500 项工作，成功率高达 98%。

相当可靠的记录，对吧？

现在想象一下，它的开发人员替换了底层模型，更改了其工具并完全重写了其执行任务的方式。

代理仍然具有相同的链上身份。

但这真的是你昨天信任的那个代理人吗？

这就是人工智能代理版本控制变得有趣的地方。

ERC-8004 提供了持久代理身份和声誉信号的框架，但身份本身并不能告诉您其背后的软件是否已更改。

这是一个非常重要的区别。

我认为未来的代理市场应该更容易追踪：

❯ 型号版本及主要更新
❯ 工具和执行环境的变化
❯ 升级前后的性能
❯ 哪个版本实际完成了每项工作

这对于像 TermiX 的 AACP 这样的东西很重要，代理可以在其中提供服务、建立声誉并参与链上交易。

版本 1.0 获得的声誉分数不应自动保证版本 2.0 的性能同样好。

当然，更新可以使代理变得更好。

重点不是阻止升级。

这是为了确保声誉反映代理今天实际可以交付的内容，而不仅仅是旧版本几个月前取得的成果。

因为持久的身份是有价值的。

但了解该身份背后发生的变化的可验证历史可能会更有用。

viral_posts.full_text_en:
I think there’s a major misunderstanding in this discussion.

The growing number of vulnerabilities discovered in open source software doesn’t necessarily mean that open source code is worse than proprietary software.

What we’re seeing is a massive increase in scrutiny.

For years, many open source projects simply didn’t receive thorough security reviews. Nobody had the time, resources or financial incentive to look that closely.

Now anyone with access to a capable LLM can point it at a public repository and start looking for vulnerabilities. And newer models are getting remarkably good at finding issues that previous tools and human reviewers missed.

But something very similar is happening behind closed doors.

I can tell you from our own experience, and from discussions with people at other software companies, that internal development teams are also struggling with a flood of findings from AI-assisted code reviews.

Many of these findings concern code that has been running in production for years. In proprietary software development, they rarely become public CVEs or security advisories. They end up as Jira tickets, creating backlogs that take weeks or months to process.

Ironically, while AI accelerates software development, it’s also slowing teams down by exposing years of accumulated technical debt and security issues that nobody had identified before.

So I’d be careful about interpreting the current wave of open source vulnerabilities as evidence of lower code quality.
viral_posts.full_text_zh:
我认为这次讨论存在重大误解。

开源软件中发现的漏洞数量不断增加并不一定意味着开源代码比专有软件更糟糕。

我们看到的是审查的大幅增加。

多年来，许多开源项目根本没有接受彻底的安全审查。没有人有时间、资源或经济动力来仔细观察。

现在，任何有权访问有能力的法学硕士的人都可以将其指向公共存储库并开始寻找漏洞。较新的模型非常擅长发现以前的工具和人工审核人员遗漏的问题。

但非常相似的事情正在幕后发生。

我可以根据我们自己的经验以及与其他软件公司人员的讨论告诉您，内部开发团队也在努力应对人工智能辅助代码审查的大量发现。

其中许多发现涉及已在生产环境中运行多年的代码。在专有软件开发中，它们很少成为公共 CVE 或安全公告。它们最终会成为 Jira 票证，造成积压，需要数周或数月的时间才能处理。

具有讽刺意味的是，虽然人工智能加速了软件开发，但它也暴露了多年来积累的技术债务和以前没有人发现的安全问题，从而减慢了团队的速度。

因此，我会谨慎地将当前的开源漏洞浪潮解释为代码质量较低的证据。
